extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of introductory/advanced single-variable calculus (undergraduate/advanced high-school)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter of a calculus textbook covering primitives, the definite integral (including improper integrals), basic integration techniques (integration by parts, change of variables), area computations (cartesian, parametric, polar), and volume formulas for solids with parallel bases and solids of revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean-value formula for integrals (formule des accroissements finis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation F(b) - F(a) = (b - a) f(ξ) for some ξ between a and b; the integral mean-value formula is identical to the finite increment formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that for a function with derivative f(x) the definite integral equals the difference of a primitive and that this can be written in the mean-value form; indicates existence of ξ in (a,b) such that the equality holds (classical mean-value result for integrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts for definite integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: For two functions u and v of x, one has ∫_a^b u(x) dv(x) = [u(x) v(x)]_a^b - ∫_a^b v(x) du(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation and explanation: the indices indicate evaluation at the limits; transposing terms yields standard definite integration by parts. Example applications to improper integrals are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket notation for difference of function values
rubrics_metrics.description: To denote the difference of values of a function F(x) at x = b and x = a, use the bracket notation F[ b ] - F[a] (i.e. F(b) - F(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compactly write expressions like [u(x)v(x)]_a^b and to express the definite integral as difference of an antiderivative at endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of integration rules to improper integrals (infinite limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules previously established (integration by parts, fundamental theorem) apply to integrals with an infinite limit provided the integrals converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the example A = ∫_0^∞ e^{-αx} sin x dx and B = ∫_0^∞ e^{-αx} cos x dx, solved by integration by parts and limit-taking; one must check convergence of the improper integrals before applying the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of variable in a definite integral (substitution rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x = φ(t) maps t from α to β to x from a to b and φ is continuously differentiable (with suitable monotonicity initially assumed), then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_α^β f(φ(t)) φ'(t) dt with adjusted limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via Riemann sums: compare corresponding partition terms and show quotient tends to 1 using derivative; initial proof assumes φ' keeps a constant sign and is later generalized by splitting the interval where φ' changes sign. Emphasizes correct transformation of limits and the differential dx = φ'(t) dt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a semicircle/ellipse via substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute areas by a judicious change of variable, e.g., for the semicircle/ellipse use x = a cos t leading to integrals in t that are easier to evaluate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows changing limits (careful with sign because dx = -a sin t dt), using trig identities (cos^2, double-angle), and evaluating definite integrals via antiderivatives; concrete calculation yields the classical area results (e.g., half-ellipse area = (πab)/2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a cycloid by parametric integration
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cycloid given by x = a(u - sin u), y = a(1 - cos u), the area under one arch is obtained by A = ∫ y dx with the curve parametrized and u ranging over one arch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change variable to u, compute dx in terms of du, expand and integrate; demonstrates that the area of one arch equals three times the area of the generating circle (classical result A = 3πa^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a closed curve via a line integral (A = ∮ y dx)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area A enclosed by a simple closed curve can be expressed as the line integral ∮_C y dx taken around the contour in the positive orientation (direction of the arrow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets the integral geometrically by summing y times the infinitesimal projection dx of displacement; shows how partitioning the curve into upper and lower arcs yields the difference of segment areas. Addresses sign conventions and how reversing orientation changes the sign of the integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric formula for area: A = ∫ y(t) x'(t) dt
rubrics_metrics.description: When the coordinates of a point M on a curve are given by x = x(t), y = y(t) and t runs from α to β describing the curve once, the area of the closed curve is A = ∫_α^β y(t) x'(t) dt (with appropriate orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the parametric form of the line integral for area; the text shows how to perform change of variable when computing area of curves presented parametrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior for curves with double points (self-intersections)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a closed contour has self-intersections (loops), the line integral ∮ y dx taken with the chosen orientation equals either the difference or the sum of the areas of the loops depending on the configuration and orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by figures: in one disposition the integral equals difference of areas of two loops (one counted negatively), in another disposition it equals the sum. The rule extends to multiple double points in the same manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential of area in polar coordinates: dA = (1/2) r^2 dθ
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve expressed in polar coordinates (r as function of θ), the differential of the area of a sector is dA = (1/2) r^2 dθ; integrating gives sector and curve areas via 1/2 ∫ r^2 dθ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by approximating the sector area by circular sectors and taking the limit; used to compute areas like the lemniscate and to express area of a curve in polar form (include care about limits and orientation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential of area in cartesian coordinates: dA = (1/2)(x dy - y dx)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalently to polar differential, for a small sector (or infinitesimal triangle) one has dA = 1/2 (x dy - y dx) and thus A = (1/2) ∮ (x dy - y dx) for a closed contour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived via coordinates of vertices of a small triangle approximating the sector; relates to the formula obtained from parametric or polar forms and to the area-as-line-integral expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of the lemniscate (example via polar integral)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the lemniscate r^2 = a^2 cos 2θ, integrate A = (1/2) ∫ r^2 dθ on appropriate θ-intervals to obtain the area of parts or the whole curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct substitution r^2 into the polar area integral yields integrals of trig expressions; constant of integration chosen so area is zero when curve shrinks to a point. The example shows using symmetry and limits in θ to compute the quarter and total curve areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic sector area and hyperbolic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: By analogy with circular sectors, the area A of a hyperbolic sector of the equilateral hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 can be used to parametrize points by a parameter t (area-related), yielding x = cosh t, y = sinh t and relations e^t = cosh t + sinh t, e^{-t} = cosh t - sinh t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows derivation of coordinates in terms of the sector area and explains why the names cosinus hyperbolique and sinus hyperbolique are appropriate; gives functional identities and points to numerical tables for values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar area formula for closed curves and origin position
rubrics_metrics.description: When a closed curve is described by r = r(θ), the area can be written as A = (1/2) ∫_{θ1}^{θ2} r^2 dθ; if the origin is interior the θ-range may be 0 to 2π, otherwise subtract sectors appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes treatment of self-intersecting curves: integral may represent sum or difference of loop areas; emphasizes correct choice of θ-interval corresponding to one traversal of the curve in the indicated orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume differential for solids with parallel bases: dV = S(z) cos θ dz
rubrics_metrics.description: For a solid whose lateral boundary is any surface and whose top and bottom are two parallel planes, let S(z) be the area of a section by a plane parallel to the bases at 'height' z; then the differential dV = S(z) cos θ dz where θ is angle between chosen axis and normal to base planes, and V = ∫ S(z) cos θ dz between the base limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: the increment of volume when z increases by Δz is trapped between cylinders of heights Δz cos θ and thus limit gives S(z) cos θ as derivative of V; remark treats modifications when projection does not cover completely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prismatoid formula (general formula for quadratic-section solids)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S(z) is a quadratic function of z (S(z)=az^2 + bz + c) then the volume between z = z0 and z = z1 is given by V = (h/6) (S0 + S1 + 4 Sm) where h is the distance between bases, S0 and S1 are base areas and Sm is the area of the middle section (at midpoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation by integrating the quadratic; notes that property is invariant under translations and rotations of axes. Special cases: if S is linear in z (a=0), this reduces to V = h/2 (S0 + S1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to elementary solids (frustum of pyramid/cone, spherical segment)
rubrics_metrics.description: These solids have cross-sectional area S(z) that is quadratic in z; thus their volumes follow from the quadratic/prismatoid formula (e.g., frustum of cone/pyramid, spherical slice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in a frustum sections are proportional to square of distances from apex, in spherical slice S(z)=π(R^2 - z^2) which is quadratic; shows how to apply the general formula to compute volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of an ellipsoid
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ellipsoid with semi-axes a, b, c, the volume is V = (4/3) π a b c (derived by treating sections parallel to a coordinate plane whose areas are quadratic in z and applying the prismatoid formula over the whole solid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take tangent planes where section area vanishes to set limits; use symmetry so middle section area is π a b and integrate or apply the quadratic formula to obtain classical result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volumes for surfaces ruled by lines (limits of polygonal constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid is generated by moving a polygonal section along many lines (or in the limit by a ruled surface), the area S of a section is quadratic (or linear) in z and the same volume formulas (prismatoid formula) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates by taking n lines intersecting a moving plane to form a polygon; the polygon area is sum of triangular areas each quadratic in z, hence S(z) quadratic; in the limit surfaces ruled with a director plane give linear cases where the simpler formula holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of solids of revolution (disk method)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve in the x-y plane (meridian) revolved about an axis (e.g., the x- or y-axis), the cross-section at a given height is a circle of radius equal to the coordinate (x or y), and the volume is V = ∫ π [radius(z)]^2 dz (i.e., V = π ∫ y(x)^2 dx when revolving around the x-axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut the solid into thin slices perpendicular to the axis of revolution; each slice is a disk (or washer) whose area is π radius^2; integrate along the axis to obtain the volume. The text begins this derivation by noting S is a circle of radius x and proceeds to integrate.
